result:
I reviewed the actual diff (not the self-report) and live-tested the wrapper scripts against the real git 2.43/gh binaries on this machine.

**Verdict: reject** (tier1 — my rejection means hold/follow-up, not autonomous merge).

What checked out: the round-4 claims about fixing the `git -C`/`--git-dir`/`gh --repo`/`-R` argv-position bypass are real — I reproduced the pre-fix bypass conceptually and confirmed the new `_interactive_guard_git_find_subcommand`/`_interactive_guard_gh_strip_globals` logic correctly detects and blocks all three previously-cited bypass commands.

What I found that sinks it: I live-tested a bypass this round didn't consider — **git/gh alias expansion**. Setting an entirely ordinary `git config alias.p push` (or any user's pre-existing custom alias) and then running `git p origin master` sails straight through the wrapper unblocked and performs a real push to `origin/master` — I verified this end-to-end against a real bare repo using the exact committed guard file and the real git 2.43 binary; the push landed, exit 0, no BLOCKED message. The wrapper only recognizes the literal token `push`/`pr merge`, with no awareness of `~/.gitconfig`'s `[alias]` section, so an alias name is treated as an "unrecognized subcommand" and passed through while the real binary still expands and executes it. Same gap class applies to `gh alias set`.

This is exactly the "real, non-obscure" bypass category this task's own four rounds have been rejecting each other over — and unlike every other residual gap in this file (absolute-path invocation, `command -p`, systemd-run impersonation, flag-allowlist staleness), it's nowhere in the otherwise very thorough KNOWN LIMITATIONS section. Given the task's whole charter is finding and either closing or honestly disclosing bypasses, this omission is reject-worthy on its own.

Wrote `review-verdict.json` at the workspace root with this verdict and the reproduction details.
